runs.text: tir, ou aprouar algũa couſa, ou conceder.

lines.note: Continues the preceding page's definition of assent: approving something or granting it. The opening tir completes the divided Portuguese verb rather than beginning a new entry.

runs.text: Porem. Vai de pois de verbo. Vt,

lines.note: This wo is an adversative particle, glossed 'however' and said to follow a verb. So- begins sonata in the example below; the separate printed de pois is retained.

Completes sonata ye mairōzuru wo: 'I would have gone there, but…'. The prospective mairǒzuru and final wo account for the Portuguese adversative explanation; the caron and abbreviation tilde are visible.
The object-marking wo is identified with the accusative. The scan prints Propoſição, which is retained rather than silently regularized to the expected grammatical term preposição.
O in the sense of a tail is matched directly by Portuguese rabo. It is a separate homographic entry from the preceding particles.
This o denotes a cord, ribbon or strap. The three Portuguese equivalents distinguish the material fastening sense from the tail entry.
Ōame denotes heavy rain, literally great rain. The headword has a visible circumflex, and chuua preserves the printed historical u/v spelling.

runs.text: Tia. Em algũas partes do Ximo,

lines.note: Oba means aunt; Ubaqi is given as a regional form in parts of Ximo. The printed Vbaqi is retained without inserting an expected o, and Ximo occurs within the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: Hũa erua que ſerue pera mezinha.

lines.note: Obako is described as an herb used medicinally. The gloss supplies the practical use without requiring a more precise botanical identification, and no long-vowel mark is added to the headword.
Ōbaku is equated with barley. The short Portuguese gloss ceuada retains its historical consonantal u.
Obamuko means an uncle by marriage, specifically the aunt's husband. The compound relation is stated explicitly in the Portuguese.

runs.text: Hũa festa que ſe faz ao Dairi, ou a

lines.note: Ōban names a feast or ceremonial offering for the Dairi or a lord named on the next row. Enlargement establishes the downward caron in Vǒban, unlike the circumflex in Vôame; Dairi is embedded in the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: algum Yacata pello Xǒguachi leuando lhe toda

lines.note: The offering is made to a yakata at the New Year, Xǒguachi, with various gifts. The o in Xǒguachi carries a caron rather than the OCR tilde; Yacata and Xǒguachi are Japanese terms within the Portuguese sentence.
Completes the feast's gifts: all kinds of game and fish. The visible a gives peſcado, correcting OCR peſcodo without modernizing the historical long s.

runs.text: Hũas meſas altas com pees, em que

lines.note: Oban here denotes tall tables or trays with feet. The scan reads altas, not OCR alias; this unaccented entry is distinct from the ceremonial Vǒban above. The supplied NINJAL index records Vôban with an editorially supplied vowel mark; no secure mark is established in this impression, so the unmarked baseline remains.
Certain lords eat at these tables. The printed algums is preserved with its historical ending rather than changed to modern alguns.

runs.text: Hũa flor de certa erua alta dos cam-

lines.note: Obana is the flower or plume of a tall field grass. The gloss is divided at cam-/pos and does not itself supply a botanical species name.
Completes campos and states that the grass serves like straw. The print appears to read panha, retained as a source anomaly rather than silently corrected to expected palha.
Obaki is another word for aunt, referred to oba. The two Japanese forms surround the Portuguese definition and cross-reference marker.

runs.text: Tio marido da propria tia: mas

lines.note: Obaki muko denotes the husband of one's own aunt. The final mas introduces a qualification about the preferred expression on the next line.
The dictionary identifies obamuko as the proper term. Vobamuco therefore occurs inside the Portuguese metalinguistic explanation rather than beginning a new entry.
Obashima is equated with rankan, a balustrade or railing. The Portuguese second equivalent continues as enco-/stos, describing a protective or supporting rail.
Completes encostos and gives balconies and bridges as locations for these railings. The inherited st/ſt expansion is retained under the project's deferred ligature policy.
Obi is a sash or girdle. Obi wo toku means undoing it, with the Portuguese desatar divided after De-.
Completes desatar, undoing the ribbon or sash; the next example, obi wo suru, means putting it on. The printed afita spacing is retained.
Cingir-se translates obi wo suru. Obi wo kumu introduces making or plaiting a sash, continued by the divided cingidouro.
The sash is made as one makes a braid. Vobi- starts another obi phrase on the following physical line.
Completes obi wo utsu, making a sash in the manner of making a cord. The comparison continues with cordão below.
Cordão completes the comparison: a cord-making technique for the sash. This brief continuation is a full physical body row.
Obi wo oru is weaving a sash, distinct from the preceding braiding and cord-making examples. Initial v in voru represents the vowel of oru.

runs.text: Vobinauoxi. i, Fibo, l, fimo vo toxi.

lines.note: Obinaoshi is equated with hibo or himo otoshi, the change from children's fastening cords to an obi. The damaged o and the printed internal space in vo toxi are retained cautiously; the clause continues as deixar on the next row.

runs.text: xar de atar o cingidouro detras como cuſtumão

lines.note: Completes deixar and explains ceasing to fasten the sash behind, as children customarily do. The gloss describes a change in dress rather than literal repair of a belt.

runs.text: os mininos ate os noue annos.

lines.note: The stated custom lasts until nine years of age. Mininos is the printed historical vowel form, not normalized to meninos.
Obikashi, with the supplied forms -su and -ita, means frightening someone. The means of frightening are supplied by the following siege example.

runs.text: gritos, ou brados como fazem os que tem de

lines.note: The frightening is done by cries or shouts. Tem de continues into cerco, describing besiegers rather than an unrelated obligation construction.

runs.text: cerco algũa fortaleza pera inquietarem os que

lines.note: Completes ter de cerco: surrounding a fortress and disturbing those within. The tilded algũa and the clause's continuation are retained.
Those inside the fortress are the people being disturbed by the shouts. This short row completes the military explanation of obikasu.

runs.text: Fazer vir, ou ſair os ini-

lines.note: Obiki means luring enemies to approach or come out. The printed abbreviated principal forms, including ijta, are retained; ini- continues as inimigos.

runs.text: migos moſtrãdolhes de lõge pouca gẽte, ou fra-

lines.note: Enemies are enticed by showing them only a small force from afar, or apparent weakness. Enlargement supports lõge and gẽte with abbreviation tildes, correcting OCR lige and ge te; fra- continues as fraqueza.
Completes fraqueza, weakness, the second deception used to lure the enemy. It belongs to obiki and remains separate from the following synonym.

Obikiidashi means luring out and is assigned the same meaning as obiki. The first o is badly abraded but its remaining bowl, the repeated stem above and the gloss support Vobiqiidaxi rather than OCR Vcbiqiidaxi. The subsequent lexical checkpoint agrees: supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, v202510, CC BY 4.0 (https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html), entry 275a21; the local scan remains the authority for the letters.
Obitadashii describes something great or overwhelming enough to cause astonishment. The Portuguese verb is divided as espanta across the row boundary.
Completes espanta muito, greatly astonishing or frightening. This is the semantic basis of the related noun and adverb printed below.
Obitadashisa is the nominal derivative, the quality or degree of being overwhelming. It is printed as an indented derivative with no separate Portuguese gloss.
Obitadashū is the adverbial derivative of obitadashii. The visible downward mark over u is retained as a caron rather than modernized to another long-vowel notation.
Obite and obitaru are presented as forms of a defective verb meaning to bear or have on oneself. The adjective-like use is illustrated by a flower carrying dew below.

Tsuyu wo obitaru hana means a flower bearing dew; the Portuguese definition continues in column 2. The enlarged image visibly prints the anomalous roaſ, apparently transposed letters for a rose, so the source order is preserved rather than silently emended to roſa.

runs.text: que tem, ou està com orualho.

lines.note: Completes the preceding column's dew-bearing flower: one that has or is covered with dew. The terminal P. is an upright poetic-use label, outside the italic Portuguese definition.
Obitori is the cord or ribbon associated with a large sword. Montante supplies the weapon context rather than a general garment sash.

runs.text: Cinta, ou lugar do cinto, ou cingi-

lines.note: Obishi denotes the waist or place where the belt is worn. The visible t gives cinto, correcting OCR cinfo; cingi- continues as cingidouro.

Completes cingidouro and begins an example about a swelling where the belt passes. The final i of touorini is abraded along a paper mark but retains part of its stem; the phrase is read as obi-shi no tōri ni, not a sentence-ending dot after touorin.
Completes haremono ga dekita: a swelling has appeared. The Portuguese describes its occurrence and continues with another term for a sore or abscess below.

runs.text: leicenſo no lugar por onde ſe hum cinge.

lines.note: The swelling or abscess is at the place around which one girds oneself. The historical printed leicenſo is retained without replacing it with a modern medical spelling.
Obiyakashi means causing fright, matching the Portuguese 'put in fear' or 'frighten'. Por is the printed form of pôr, and the abbreviated eſpãtar is not expanded.

runs.text: O eſtar como doente ſem calçoẽs,

lines.note: Ōbyakutan is explained as being dressed like an invalid, without breeches. The worn first vowel after ç in calçoẽs is retained from the aligned reading; the following e bears the abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: & mal compoſto como pera ver alguem, &c.

lines.note: Continues the description of inadequate or disordered dress when seeing someone. The Portuguese wording is retained as printed rather than supplying an unstated negation.
Ōbyakue is assigned the same clothing or undress sense as the preceding entry. Idem is an explicit cross-reference, not an independent explanation.
Obie means becoming frightened or startled. The Portuguese adds a state resembling being beside oneself, completed on the next row.
Fora de si completes the description of being beside oneself from fright. The printed deſi remains joined in the transcription.

Obie-agari intensifies the preceding verb: to become very frightened. The scan visibly prints the anomalous principal part arta, retained rather than emended to expected atta; OCR also garbled Eſpantarſe muito.
The second paraphrase is to be left as though stunned or astonished. It completes the intensified fright definition.

Obie-tamagiri receives the same meaning of being greatly frightened. The far-right '(Rey.' is physically on this row but completes 'Leis, ou ordenaçoens do' in the following entry; it is preserved in its printed location with explicit far-right spans, not treated as part of Idẽ.

Ōbō is explained by ō no nori, laws or ordinances of the king; the displaced Rey. is above at the far right. The first headword mark is faint but compatible with a caron, while its final o clearly has a circumflex; the mixed Vǒbô and Vǒno are preserved rather than normalized.
Obore means drowning in water. The gloss offers an additional, less final description on the next line rather than limiting the word to death.

runs.text: verſe em aperto de baixo dagoa. Vt,

lines.note: The second explanation is finding oneself in distress beneath water. Vt introduces the Japanese example, and the historical joined dagoa remains unchanged.
Mizu ni oboruru illustrates drowning or struggling in water. The printed zz belongs to the dictionary's Japanese spelling, and oboruru is the historical form rather than modern oboreru.
Ōbori and ōhori are alternative forms for a large ditch or excavation. Latin l introduces the alternative, and both printed circumflexes are preserved.
Oboro or oborona describes something only indistinctly visible. The final mark after eſcaſamẽ is a line-division hyphen, correcting the OCR period.

runs.text: te ſe vè, ou couſa enneuoada.

lines.note: Completes escasamente and adds the sense of something clouded or misty. The physical row continues the adjective's definition rather than introducing a new adverb.
Oboroni is the adverb; the Permet marker introduces a transferred use. Vobo- begins the example of knowing something indistinctly.
Completes oboroni mono wo shiru: to know something poorly or vaguely. The Portuguese specifies insufficient clarity on the next line.
Little clarity and distinction complete the figurative knowledge example. The sense is uncertain understanding, not bad conduct.
Oboroke and oborokena are alternative forms for something faintly apparent or slight. The first Portuguese gloss is split as eſca-/ſamente.
Completes the description of something barely visible or small in amount. These are the two senses subsequently illustrated adverbially.
Oborokeni is the adverb, glossed escasamente. The tall unbarred initial s corrects OCR Efcaſamente; Itẽ introduces a second nuance.
The second gloss is 'little' or in a borrowed, provisional manner. Vobo- begins the following negative example rather than forming part of the Portuguese phrase.
Completes oborokeni mo shiranu, not knowing even a little. The Portuguese diminutive is divided ta-/manino across the physical lines.
Completes tamanino, a very small amount. Together with the preceding negative it means not knowing the least bit.
Oborozuki is a clouded or hazy moon. The printed zz and tilded Lũa are retained, while the second description continues below.
Completes the description of a moon that appears only faintly. The inherited accented apàrece is retained; the small mark lies near a paper blemish and is less secure than the lexical letters.
Oborozukiyo is a dim moonlit night. The Portuguese first says a night with little brightness, then specifies the moonlight itself below.
Dim moonlight completes the definition of oborozukiyo. The abbreviation tilde remains on u in lũar.
Obotsukanai describes something doubtful or uncertain. The Portuguese double u in duuidoſa is retained as historical spelling.
Obotsukanasa is the corresponding noun for uncertainty or doubt. It is an indented derivative, with the preceding gloss supplying its sense.
Obotsukanō is the adverbial form, explicitly marked Adu. The visible caron is preserved, rather than replacing the historical form with modern obotsukanaku.
Oboshi means thinking or loving and points to the fuller honorific expression below. The supplied -su and -shita principal forms remain unexpanded.
The cross-reference is to oboshimeshi, oboshimesu, immediately below. Infrà belongs to the italic explanatory apparatus; the Japanese verb is the cited target.
Oboshimeshi is glossed as thinking or loving, followed by a Japanese equivalent in the next row. The italic i introduces that explanatory equivalence.
Omoi/omou supplies the nonhonorific equivalent. The Portuguese calls oboshimesu an honorific verb and begins an additional remark at ain-/da.

runs.text: da fica mais honrado com, rare. Vt,

lines.note: The verb becomes still more honorific with rare, the Japanese auxiliary cited inside the Portuguese explanation. Honrado corrects OCR hourado; Voboxi- begins the resulting example.
Completes oboshimesare, with -uru as the further principal form. The printed long s in meſare is retained rather than made uniform with the x in the headword.

runs.text: Voboximexi cauaxi, ſu, ita. i, Vomoi ca-

lines.note: Oboshimeshi-kawashi is explained by omoi-kawasu, mutual affection. The headword's second x is visible, correcting OCR Voboximesi; ca- continues on the next line.
Completes omoi-kawasu and gives the meaning 'to love one another'. The unbarred tall letter is long ſ, not OCR f, consistent with the verb ending -su.

runs.text: Voboximexi caye, uru, eta. i, Vomoi ca-

lines.note: Oboshimeshi-kae is equated with omoi-kayuru, continued by yuru. at the opening of the supplied following page f542. The bottom yuru. is the anticipatory catchword and is not counted again as body text here.
